parts.text:
You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: As a dispatcher, I plan and run the flights for my company, and I am the licensed person responsible for each flight. I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves or call it off. Several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, so I need help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. My policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for me.
The question: How do you plan and sign off a flight, and what information or validation does the service need to provide?

Q3
The answer just before it: I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves, though I can also call it off. Software never chooses a drone or a way for me, as that is against our policy and my legal responsibility. I do want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts.
The question: What rules or conflicts can occur when several dispatchers plan at the same time for the same sites and drones?

Q4
The answer just before it: Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and the same popular drones. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. I don't know.
The question: What details are required to define a job, flight, or corridor, and what happens when you sign off or call off a flight?

Q5
The answer just before it: Deliveries carry a load from one site to another, and inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started. Drones fly along corridors between named sites. As a dispatcher, I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves or call it off.
The question: What information about drones does the service need to consider when helping you find which drones can get to a job's start?

Q6
The answer just before it: The drones are of several models from different manufacturers, and they differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned. Each drone has a home site, and each company has its own charging pads at its own sites.
The question: How does weather, such as cold and wind, or battery drain affect planning or sign-off?

Q7
The answer just before it: Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned. I don't know.
The question: What kinds of jobs do customer companies run, and what requirements do they have?

Q8
The answer just before it: Deliveries carry a load from one site to another, and inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started. The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do, and each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.
The question: When you ask the service for help finding which drones can get to a job start, what does it show or check?

Q9
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Can two dispatchers assign the same drone or the same takeoff/landing spot at the same time? How should conflicts be handled?

Q10
The answer just before it: Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and the same popular drones. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. I don't know.
The question: What happens to a planned or in-flight mission when an airspace closure affects its corridor or zone?

Q11
The answer just before it: The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves. A closure can even come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.
The question: What sites exist, and does each company only use its own sites or are sites shared?

Q12
The answer just before it: Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and each company has its own charging pads at its own sites. These sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. Pads are never lent to another company.
The question: How does the service help you sign off a flight before it leaves, and what checks must pass?
